That’s the full testing vocabulary for the Reducer pattern:
-keypaths for child stores, and closures or injected fakes for anything more
specific. All of it runs against production reducer code — there’s nothing test-only
. Closures let you assert on multiple
properties at once, verify side effects on injected fakes, or express the acceptance
criteria for a whole user-facing feature as a single readable test.

In complex applications, managing all state and events in a single Statostore quickly becomes unsustainable. To scale effectively, we need to split the app’s state and events into separate parts or Scopes. This process can sometimes be straightforward, but other times, developers may feel compelled to separate state and events that are closely tied together due to business logic. In this tutorial, we’ll focus on how to organize app state into different scopes to maintain scalability.

Learn how to easily design dependencies and inject them into your scopes. Dependency injection simplifies the structure of your code by externalizing the management of dependencies, making your code more modular, testable, and flexible. In this tutorial, we will demonstrate dependency injection using an example of a simple news feed application.

/// `WHEN_EffectCompletes` (see below) needs to look an effect up by its own type, and a bare
/// closure has no nameable type of its own: every `AnyEffect { ... }.map(...)` with the same
/// `ResultType` is indistinguishable from any other. Reach for a named `Effect` conformance
/// whenever a test needs to target one specifically.
